docs.title: twotower
docs.text: A two-tower retrieval model for recommendations, with a scikit-learn–style API.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install twotower

For the optional FastAPI / Gradio serving layer:

pip install "twotower[app]"

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from twotower import TwoTower, split_interactions

# Load your interactions (must have event_date, user_id, item_id, clicks columns)
interactions = pd.read_csv("interactions.csv")

# Split by date into train / validation / test
train_df, valid_df, test_df = split_interactions(interactions)

# Separate features from labels
X_train, y_train = train_df.drop(columns=["clicks"]), train_df["clicks"]
X_valid, y_valid = valid_df.drop(columns=["clicks"]), valid_df["clicks"]

# Train
model = TwoTower(epochs=10)
model.fit(
    X_train=X_train, y_train=y_train,
    X_valid=X_valid, y_valid=y_valid,
)

# Predict top-10 items for a list of users
recommendations = model.predict(user_ids=[1, 2, 3], top_k=10)

# Evaluate recall on held-out test data
metrics = model.evaluate(test_df)

# Persist
model.save_model("model.pth")
model.load_model("model.pth")

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
twotower follows the fit → predict → evaluate pattern familiar from scikit-learn.

  • User tower and item tower each map an entity ID (plus optional side features) through an MLP to a shared embedding space.
  • At inference time, user and item embeddings are compared with a dot product; the top-k items are returned per user.
  • Training uses Bayesian Personalised Ranking (BPR) loss with optional in-batch InfoNCE contrastive loss.

docs.title: twotower.TwoTower
docs.text:
Bases: TwoTowerBase

Two-tower retrieval model with a scikit-learn–style API.

Both towers share the same MLP architecture and embed users and items into a common hidden_dim-dimensional space. Similarity is measured with a dot product. Training minimises BPR loss with optional in-batch InfoNCE contrastive loss.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default user_col str

Column name for user IDs in the interaction DataFrames.

'user_id' item_col str

Column name for item IDs in the interaction DataFrames.

'banner_id' user_embedding_dim int

Dimensionality of the learned user ID embedding.

64 item_embedding_dim int

Dimensionality of the learned item ID embedding.

64 side_feature_embedding_dim int

Dimensionality of each side-feature embedding.

8 hidden_dim int

Output embedding size for both towers.

64 tower_dims tuple[int, ...]

Hidden layer sizes for the MLP inside each tower. Each layer is followed by BatchNorm1d, ReLU, and optional Dropout. Pass an empty tuple () for a single linear projection.

(128, 64) dropout float

Dropout rate applied after each hidden layer in the MLP. Must be in [0, 1).

0.0 retrieval_temperature float

Temperature for the in-batch InfoNCE loss.

0.1 learning_rate float

Adam optimizer learning rate.

0.001 weight_decay float

L2 regularization coefficient for the Adam optimizer. Helps prevent overfitting on small datasets.

0.0 batch_size int

Mini-batch size for training.

2048 epochs int

Maximum number of training epochs.

25 eval_top_ks tuple[int, ...]

Top-k values used when computing recall metrics.

(50, 100, 300) max_eval_users int

Maximum number of users sampled for evaluation.

500 top_k int

Default number of recommendations returned by predict.

100 eval_during_training bool

Whether to compute recall metrics after each epoch.

True seed int

Random seed for reproducibility.

42 device str | None

PyTorch device string ("cpu", "cuda"), or None to auto-detect.

'cpu' Example 
from twotower import TwoTower, split_interactions

train_df, valid_df, test_df = split_interactions(interactions_df)

model = TwoTower(epochs=10, tower_dims=(128, 64))
model.fit(train_df, validation_data=valid_df)
recommendations = model.predict(user_ids=[1, 2, 3], top_k=10)
metrics = model.evaluate(test_df)
model.save_model("model.pth")

docs.title: twotower.split_interactions(interactions_df, validation_ratio=0.2, test_ratio=0.1)
docs.text:
Split an interactions DataFrame into train, validation, and test sets.

The split is temporal: all interactions from a date are kept together, and dates are assigned to the split whose row-count target they best match. This prevents future leakage into the training set.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default interactions_df DataFrame

DataFrame with at least an event_date column. All other columns are preserved unchanged.

required validation_ratio float

Approximate fraction of rows to assign to validation. Must be in [0, 1).

0.2 test_ratio float

Approximate fraction of rows to assign to test. Must be in [0, 1).

0.1

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

A 3-tuple (train_df, valid_df, test_df), each sorted by

DataFrame

event_date with the original columns intact.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the DataFrame is empty, missing event_date, has fewer than 3 unique dates, or if the ratio arguments are invalid.

Example 
train_df, valid_df, test_df = split_interactions(
    interactions_df,
    validation_ratio=0.15,
    test_ratio=0.10,
)

docs.title: twotower.FeatureConfig dataclass
docs.text: Declares which columns to encode as side features.

docs.title: twotower.MultiFeatureSpec dataclass
docs.text: Describes a single multi-valued feature and its source columns.

docs.title: twotower.NegativeSampling dataclass
docs.text:
Negative sampling strategy passed to fit().

Controls how negative examples are drawn during training. observed_ratio sets the fraction of negatives sampled from observed non-positive interactions (vs random items). in_batch_loss_weight adds an InfoNCE contrastive loss over the batch similarity matrix on top of BPR; set to 0.0 to disable.

docs.title: twotower.EarlyStopping dataclass
docs.text:
Early stopping strategy passed to fit().

Monitors metric after every epoch and halts training when it does not improve by more than min_delta for patience consecutive epochs. Metric mode (min/max) is inferred automatically: loss metrics use min, recall metrics use max.

docs.title: Expected format
docs.text: Three CSV files are needed: interactions, users (optional), and items (optional).

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text:
The interactions table records every user–item event:

Column Type Description event_date date / datetime When the event occurred user_id int User identifier item_id int Item identifier (configurable) clicks int Number of clicks (> 0 → positive label)

The column names for user and item are configurable via user_col / item_col when constructing TwoTower. The event_date column is always required by name.

docs.title: Users and items (side features)
docs.text:
Side-feature tables are flat CSVs with one row per entity:

user_id, age_group, country
1001, 25-34, US
1002, 18-24, DE

All columns are treated as categorical strings. See Training → Side features for how to declare them.

docs.title: Splitting by date
docs.text:
split_interactions performs a temporal split — it never leaks future events into the training set:

from twotower import split_interactions

train_df, valid_df, test_df = split_interactions(
    interactions_df,
    validation_ratio=0.2,
    test_ratio=0.1,
)

The function finds the date boundaries that best match the requested ratios, keeping all interactions from a given date in the same split. It requires at least 3 unique event dates.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description validation_ratio 0.2 Fraction of interactions for validation test_ratio 0.1 Fraction of interactions for test

docs.title: Returns
docs.text: A 3-tuple (train_df, valid_df, test_df) — each is a slice of the original DataFrame sorted by event_date.

docs.title: Loading data
docs.text:
A typical loading pattern:

import pandas as pd
from twotower import split_interactions

interactions = pd.read_csv("interactions.csv")
users = pd.read_csv("users.csv")
items = pd.read_csv("items.csv")

train_df, valid_df, test_df = split_interactions(interactions)

Then pass the splits directly to TwoTower.fit:

X_train = train_df.drop(columns=["clicks"])
y_train = train_df["clicks"]

X_valid = valid_df.drop(columns=["clicks"])
y_valid = valid_df["clicks"]

docs.title: evaluate
docs.text:
metrics = model.evaluate(X_test)

evaluate computes retrieval metrics on a held-out test set. X_test must contain the same user and item ID columns used during training, plus either a clicks or label column.

# With a clicks column — label is derived as (clicks > 0)
metrics = model.evaluate(test_df)

# With an explicit label column (0.0 / 1.0 floats)
metrics = model.evaluate(test_df.rename(columns={"clicks": "label"}))

# Evaluate at a custom top-k
metrics = model.evaluate(test_df, top_k=50)

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
A dict with the following keys (top-k values come from eval_top_ks plus top_k):

{
    "recall_at_50":  0.34,
    "recall_at_100": 0.41,
    "popularity_recall_at_50": 0.28,   # baseline: recommend most popular items
    "popularity_recall_at_100": 0.33,
}

docs.title: Recall@k
docs.text:
Recall@k measures the fraction of relevant items that appear in the top-k recommendations, averaged over users:

$$\text{Recall@k} = \frac{1}{|U|} \sum_{u \in U} \frac{|\text{recommended}_u \cap \text{relevant}_u|}{|\text{relevant}_u|}$$

Seen items (interactions from the training set) are excluded from the recommendation list by default.

docs.title: Popularity baseline
docs.text: popularity_recall_at_k is a naïve baseline that recommends the globally most popular training items to every user (seen items excluded). Values above the baseline indicate the model has learned personalised signal beyond simple popularity.

docs.title: Configuring evaluation
docs.text:
These parameters on TwoTower control how evaluation is performed:

Parameter Default Description eval_top_ks (50, 100, 300) Top-k values to evaluate during training and in evaluate() max_eval_users 500 Maximum number of users sampled for evaluation (for speed) eval_during_training True Whether to compute recall metrics after each training epoch

docs.title: Training history
docs.text:
After fit, the full per-epoch history is available:

history = model.fit(...)

for epoch in history:
    print(epoch)
# {'epoch': 1, 'train_loss': 0.62, 'valid_loss': 0.58, 'recall_at_100': 0.12, ...}

docs.title: predict
docs.text:
recommendations = model.predict(
    user_ids=[1001, 1002, 1003],
    top_k=10,
)

Returns a dict mapping each user ID to their ranked list of recommendations:

{
    1001: [{"item_id": 42, "score": 0.97}, {"item_id": 7, "score": 0.94}, ...],
    1002: [...],
}

The item key in each dict matches the item_col used when constructing the model (defaults to "banner_id").

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description user_ids None User IDs to predict for. If None, up to 10 known users are used. item_ids None Candidate item IDs. If None, all known items are candidates. top_k None Number of items to return per user. Falls back to the model's top_k config value. exclude_seen True Whether to exclude items the user interacted with in training. strict False If True, raises an error for unknown user or item IDs. If False, they are silently skipped.

docs.title: Restricting the candidate pool
docs.text:
Pass item_ids to predict from a subset of items:

# Only consider items in a specific category
candidate_ids = items_df.loc[items_df["category"] == "electronics", "item_id"].tolist()
recommendations = model.predict(user_ids=[1001], item_ids=candidate_ids, top_k=5)

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
A fitted model can be persisted and reloaded:

# Save
model.save_model("model.pth")

# Load into a fresh instance
model2 = TwoTower()
model2.load_model("model.pth")

# Or use method chaining
model2 = TwoTower().load_model("model.pth")

recommendations = model2.predict(user_ids=[1001])

The checkpoint stores the model weights, config, ID mappings, training history, and side-feature metadata. Side-feature DataFrames are not saved; the embeddings baked into the tower weights are preserved.

docs.title: Basic training
docs.text:
from twotower import TwoTower

model = TwoTower(
    epochs=25,
    batch_size=2048,
    tower_dims=(256, 128),
)

history = model.fit(
    X_train=X_train, y_train=y_train,
    X_valid=X_valid, y_valid=y_valid,
)

fit returns the training history — a list of dicts with per-epoch metrics (train loss, valid loss, recall@k).

docs.title: Key hyperparameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description user_col "user_id" Column name for user IDs in your DataFrame item_col "banner_id" Column name for item IDs in your DataFrame tower_dims (256, 128) MLP hidden layer sizes for both towers. Empty tuple () for a linear projection. hidden_dim 64 Output embedding dimension dropout 0.0 Dropout rate applied inside the MLP towers retrieval_temperature 0.1 Softmax temperature for in-batch InfoNCE loss learning_rate 1e-3 Adam optimizer learning rate batch_size 2048 Training mini-batch size epochs 25 Maximum number of training epochs max_samples 250_000 Cap on the number of positive training pairs; None to use all seed 42 Random seed for reproducibility device "cpu" "cpu", "cuda", or None (auto-detect)

docs.title: Tower architecture
docs.text:
Each tower follows the same architecture:

ID embedding  ──┐
side features ──┴─▶  concat  ──▶  MLP  ──▶  LayerNorm  ──▶  embedding

tower_dims controls the MLP hidden layers. Each hidden layer applies:

  1. Linear
  2. BatchNorm1d
  3. ReLU
  4. Dropout (if dropout > 0)

The final linear projects to hidden_dim, followed by LayerNorm.

docs.title: Negative sampling
docs.text:
Control how negative examples are constructed during training:

from twotower import NegativeSampling

model.fit(
    ...,
    negative_sampling=NegativeSampling(
        observed_ratio=0.8,       # 80 % from observed non-positive interactions
        in_batch_loss_weight=0.5, # add InfoNCE in-batch contrastive loss
    ),
)
Parameter Default Description observed_ratio 0.8 Fraction of negatives drawn from observed (non-positive) items vs. random items in_batch_loss_weight 0.0 Weight for the InfoNCE in-batch contrastive loss; 0.0 disables it

docs.title: Early stopping
docs.text:
Early stopping is enabled by default and monitors validation loss:

from twotower import EarlyStopping

model.fit(
    ...,
    early_stopping=EarlyStopping(
        patience=5,
        metric="valid_loss",  # or e.g. "recall_at_100"
        min_delta=1e-4,
    ),
)

Pass early_stopping=None to train for the full epochs.

Parameter Default Description patience 5 Stop after this many epochs without improvement metric "valid_loss" Metric to monitor; loss metrics minimise, recall_at_* maximise min_delta 1e-4 Minimum improvement to count as progress

docs.title: Side features
docs.text:
Pass side-feature DataFrames and declare which columns to use:

from twotower import TwoTower, FeatureConfig, MultiFeatureSpec

model = TwoTower()

model.fit(
    X_train=X_train, y_train=y_train,
    X_valid=X_valid, y_valid=y_valid,
    users_df=users_df,
    items_df=items_df,
    user_feature_config=FeatureConfig(
        scalar_features=("country", "age_group"),
    ),
    item_feature_config=FeatureConfig(
        scalar_features=("category",),
        multi_features=(
            MultiFeatureSpec(name="tags", columns=("tag_1", "tag_2", "tag_3")),
        ),
    ),
)

users_df and items_df must be provided together. They must contain an ID column matching user_col / item_col.

docs.title: FeatureConfig
docs.text: Parameter Description scalar_features Tuple of column names, each encoded as a single embedding multi_features Tuple of MultiFeatureSpec, each pooled across its columns

docs.title: MultiFeatureSpec
docs.text: Parameter Description name Feature name (used for embedding tables) columns Tuple of column names holding the values for this feature
